topic: Engine inspection, records and approved data

notes.front: What is an engine life-limited part under 33.70?
notes.back: A rotor or major static structural part of the engine whose primary failure is likely to result in a hazardous engine effect.
notes.explanation: Part 33 singles these parts out by the consequence of their failure: a hazardous engine effect.
notes.evidence: Engine life-limited parts are rotor and major static structural parts whose primary failure is likely to result in a hazardous engine effect.
notes.example: Like the life-limited parts met in General, but specifically the engine’s rotating and major static structural parts, with lives counted in flight cycles.

notes.front: What is time between overhauls (TBO)?
notes.back: The maximum expected time before overhaul: the span of time within which an engine needs to be overhauled.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the manufacturer sets engine removal times, and TBO is established from service experience.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine or Component Lifespan Exceeded”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: Thus, the manufacturer sets engine removal times. Based on service experience, it is possible to establish a maximum expected time before overhaul (TBO) or span of time within which an engine needs to be overhauled.
notes.example: Like a car’s recommended service interval, but marking when the whole engine is due for overhaul.

notes.front: What is a spectrometric oil analysis program (SOAP)?
notes.back: A program that analyses an oil sample for minute metallic elements, the wear metals that oil in service picks up.
notes.explanation: Because oil circulates throughout the engine, every lubricant in service carries microscopic wear metals, so a sample reflects the engine’s insides.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spectrometric Oil Analysis Engine Inspection Program”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: Spectrometric oil analysis program allows an oil sample to be analyzed and searched for the presence of minute metallic elements. Due to oil circulation throughout an aircraft engine, every lubricant that is in service contains microscopic particles of metallic elements called wear metals.
notes.example: Like a blood test that shows a problem before symptoms appear, but for engine oil.

notes.front: What is the engine mount on most reciprocating-engine aircraft?
notes.back: A welded steel-tube structure, in one or more sections, with an engine mount ring, bracing members (V-struts) and fittings to the nacelle.
notes.explanation: The handbook describes the mount as the structure whose fittings attach it to the wing nacelle while the ring carries the engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Mounts for Reciprocating Engines”, p. 8-16
notes.evidence: Most aircraft equipped with reciprocating engines use an engine mount structure made of welded steel tubing. The mount is constructed in one or more sections that incorporate the engine mount ring, bracing members (V-struts), and fittings for attaching the mount to the wing nacelle.
notes.example: Like the frame that holds a motorbike engine in place, but a truss of welded steel tubes.

notes.front: What is a vibration isolator in an engine installation?
notes.back: A flexible, or elastic, shock mount of rubber and steel that permits restricted engine movement in all directions.
notes.explanation: The handbook says larger, more powerful engines needed some way to absorb their vibration, and rubber-and-steel shock mounts were developed for it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Turbine Vibration Isolation Engine Mounts”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: As aircraft engines became larger and produced more power, some method was needed to absorb their vibration. This demand led to the development of the rubber and steel enginesuspension units called shock mounts. This combination permits restricted engine movement in all directions. These vibration isolators are commonly known as flexible, or elastic, shock mounts.
notes.example: Like the rubber bushes under a washing machine, but carrying an aircraft engine.

notes.front: What is a dynafocal mount?
notes.back: An engine mount unit (a vibration isolator) giving directional support, with its mounting pad angled to point at the engine’s centre of gravity.
notes.explanation: Angling each pad towards the centre of gravity of the engine’s mass is what gives the support its direction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Mounts for Reciprocating Engines”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: Dynafocal engine mounts, or vibration isolators, are units that give directional support to the engines. Dynafocal engine mounts have the mounting pad angled to point to the CG of the engines mass.
notes.example: Like table legs that all lean in towards one point, but each pad aims at the engine’s centre of gravity.

notes.front: What does a turbofan engine mount do?
notes.back: It supports the engine and transmits the loads the engine imposes to the aircraft structure; most are stainless steel.
notes.explanation: The handbook says these are the same basic functions as any engine mount, even though turbine mounts are usually stainless steel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Mounts for Turbofan Engines”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: The engine mounts on most turbofan engines perform the same basic functions of supporting the engine and transmitting the loads imposed by the engine to the aircraft structure. Most turbine engine mounts are made of stainless steel
notes.example: Like a piston engine’s mount in purpose, but built for a turbofan.

notes.front: What is a cylinder compression test?
notes.back: A test of whether the valves, piston rings and pistons are adequately sealing the combustion chamber.
notes.explanation: If pressure leakage past these parts is excessive, the cylinder cannot develop its full power.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Compression Tests”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: The cylinder compression test determines if the valves, piston rings, and pistons are adequately sealing the combustion chamber. If pressure leakage is excessive, the cylinder cannot develop its full power.
notes.example: Like checking a tyre for a slow leak, but on a cylinder with its valves closed.

notes.front: What is a differential compression test?
notes.back: A compression check made with a differential pressure tester, which measures the leakage through the cylinders.
notes.explanation: Measuring leakage lets it detect minute valve leaks, so cylinders can be replaced where valve burning is starting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Differential Pressure Tester”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: The differential pressure tester checks the compression of aircraft engines by measuring the leakage through the cylinders. The design of this compression tester is such that minute valve leakages can be detected, making possible the replacement of cylinders where valve burning is starting.
notes.example: Like any cylinder compression test, but reading how much air leaks away rather than how much pressure the piston builds.

notes.front: In the engine run required by 43.15(c)(2), which item is judged by static and idle rpm?
notes.back: Power output.
notes.explanation: The rule measures power output through two readings, static rpm and idle rpm, against the manufacturer’s recommendations.
notes.evidence: (i) Power output (static and idle r.p.m.);

notes.front: In the engine run required by 43.15(c)(2), which ignition item must show satisfactory performance?
notes.back: The magnetos.
notes.explanation: The magnetos are the second of the four items the run must show satisfactory, after power output.
notes.evidence: (i) Power output (static and idle r.p.m.); (ii) Magnetos;

notes.front: In the engine run required by 43.15(c)(2), which two pressures must be satisfactory?
notes.back: Fuel pressure and oil pressure.
notes.explanation: Fuel and oil pressure form one item of the four, judged against the manufacturer’s recommendations.
notes.evidence: (iii) Fuel and oil pressure; and

notes.front: In the engine run required by 43.15(c)(2), which two temperatures must be satisfactory?
notes.back: Cylinder temperature and oil temperature.
notes.explanation: Cylinder and oil temperature are the last of the four items the run checks.
notes.evidence: (iv) Cylinder and oil temperature.

notes.front: Each person performing an annual or 100-hour inspection shall use a {{c1::checklist}} while performing the inspection.
notes.back: checklist
notes.explanation: Section 43.15(c)(1) makes the checklist mandatory for these two inspections and sets appendix D as its minimum scope.
notes.evidence: Each person performing an annual or 100-hour inspection shall use a checklist while performing the inspection. The checklist may be of the person's own design, one provided by the manufacturer of the equipment being inspected or one obtained from another source. This checklist must include the scope and detail of the items contained in appendix D

notes.front: Under appendix D(d) to part 43, what must the engine section be inspected for?
notes.back: Visual evidence of excessive oil, fuel or hydraulic leaks, and the sources of such leaks.
notes.explanation: Appendix D asks for the source of a leak as well as the leak itself, so tracing it is part of the inspection.
notes.evidence: (1) Engine section—for visual evidence of excessive oil, fuel, or hydraulic leaks, and sources of such leaks.

notes.front: Under appendix D(d) to part 43, what must engine studs and nuts be inspected for?
notes.back: Improper torquing and obvious defects.
notes.explanation: Appendix D names torque specifically for studs and nuts, alongside any obvious defect.
notes.evidence: (2) Studs and nuts—for improper torquing and obvious defects.

notes.front: Under appendix D(d) to part 43, what must the engine mount be inspected for?
notes.back: Cracks, looseness of mounting, and looseness of engine to mount.
notes.explanation: Appendix D separates looseness of the mount itself from looseness of the engine on the mount, so both are checked.
notes.evidence: (4) Engine mount—for cracks, looseness of mounting, and looseness of engine to mount.

notes.front: Under appendix D(d) to part 43, what must flexible vibration dampeners be inspected for?
notes.back: Poor condition and deterioration.
notes.explanation: Appendix D lists them as their own item, checked for poor condition and deterioration.
notes.evidence: (5) Flexible vibration dampeners—for poor condition and deterioration.

notes.front: Under appendix D(d) to part 43, what must the engine controls be inspected for?
notes.back: Defects, improper travel, and improper safetying.
notes.explanation: Appendix D covers how far the controls move and how they are safetied, not just visible defects.
notes.evidence: (6) Engine controls—for defects, improper travel, and improper safetying.

notes.front: Under appendix D(d) to part 43, what must lines, hoses and clamps be inspected for?
notes.back: Leaks, improper condition and looseness.
notes.explanation: Appendix D groups lines, hoses and clamps as one item and checks them for leaks as well as condition and looseness.
notes.evidence: (7) Lines, hoses, and clamps—for leaks, improper condition and looseness.

notes.front: Under appendix D(d) to part 43, what must engine accessories be inspected for?
notes.back: Apparent defects in security of mounting.
notes.explanation: For accessories, appendix D focuses on how securely they are mounted.
notes.evidence: (9) Accessories—for apparent defects in security of mounting.

notes.front: Appendix D(d)(10): All systems—for improper installation, {{c1::poor general condition}}, defects, and insecure attachment.
notes.back: poor general condition
notes.explanation: The all-systems item is the catch-all of the engine and nacelle group, covering installation, general condition, defects and attachment.
notes.evidence: (10) All systems—for improper installation, poor general condition, defects, and insecure attachment.

notes.front: Under appendix D(d) to part 43, what must the cowling be inspected for?
notes.back: Cracks and defects.
notes.explanation: The cowling is the last item of the engine and nacelle group, checked for cracks and defects only.
notes.evidence: (11) Cowling—for cracks, and defects.

notes.front: Under appendix D(d)(3) to part 43, what must the internal engine be inspected for?
notes.back: Cylinder compression, and metal particles or foreign matter on screens and sump drain plugs.
notes.explanation: This item is where the compression check and the look at screens and sump plugs enter the annual and 100-hour inspection.
notes.evidence: (3) Internal engine—for cylinder compression and for metal particles or foreign matter on screens and sump drain plugs.

notes.front: Appendix D(h)(1): Propeller assembly—for cracks, nicks, binds, and {{c1::oil leakage}}.
notes.back: oil leakage
notes.explanation: The propeller assembly item looks for damage, binding and oil leakage.
notes.evidence: (1) Propeller assembly—for cracks, nicks, binds, and oil leakage.

notes.front: Under appendix D(h) to part 43, what must propeller anti-icing devices be inspected for?
notes.back: Improper operations and obvious defects.
notes.explanation: For anti-icing devices appendix D looks at how they operate as well as visible defects.
notes.evidence: (3) Anti-icing devices—for improper operations and obvious defects.

notes.front: Under appendix D(h) to part 43, what must propeller control mechanisms be inspected for?
notes.back: Improper operation, insecure mounting, and restricted travel.
notes.explanation: Control mechanisms are checked for how they work, how they are mounted and how far they travel.
notes.evidence: (4) Control mechanisms—for improper operation, insecure mounting, and restricted travel.

notes.front: When are the alterations listed in appendix A(a)(2) to part 43 powerplant major alterations?
notes.back: When they are not listed in the engine specifications issued by the FAA.
notes.explanation: The engine specifications decide it: the same change listed there is not a powerplant major alteration under this paragraph.
notes.evidence: The following alterations of a powerplant when not listed in the engine specifications issued by the FAA, are powerplant major alterations.

notes.front: Appendix A(a)(2)(i): Conversion of an aircraft engine from one approved model to another, involving any changes in {{c1::compression ratio}}, propeller reduction gear, impeller gear ratios or the substitution of major engine parts which requires extensive rework and testing, is a powerplant major alteration.
notes.back: compression ratio
notes.explanation: Model conversions count as major when they change these design features or need major parts with extensive rework and testing.
notes.evidence: (i) Conversion of an aircraft engine from one approved model to another, involving any changes in compression ratio, propeller reduction gear, impeller gear ratios or the substitution of major engine parts which requires extensive rework and testing of the engine.

notes.front: Under appendix A(a)(2)(ii), when is replacing engine structural parts a powerplant major alteration?
notes.back: When the replacements are not supplied by the original manufacturer or not specifically approved by the Administrator.
notes.explanation: The test is the origin or approval of the replacement structural part.
notes.evidence: (ii) Changes to the engine by replacing aircraft engine structural parts with parts not supplied by the original manufacturer or parts not specifically approved by the Administrator.

notes.front: Under appendix A(a)(2)(iv), when is removing an accessory a powerplant major alteration?
notes.back: When the accessory is listed as required equipment on the aircraft or engine specification.
notes.explanation: The test is whether the aircraft or engine specification lists the accessory as required equipment.
notes.evidence: (iv) Removal of accessories that are listed as required equipment on the aircraft or engine specification.

notes.front: Under appendix A(a)(2)(v), which installation of structural parts is a powerplant major alteration?
notes.back: Installing structural parts other than the type of parts approved for the installation.
notes.explanation: Item (v) concerns the type of structural part approved for the installation, whoever supplied it.
notes.evidence: (v) Installation of structural parts other than the type of parts approved for the installation.

notes.front: Under appendix A(a)(2)(vi), which fuel-related change is a powerplant major alteration?
notes.back: Any conversion to use fuel of a rating or grade other than the one listed in the engine specifications.
notes.explanation: The engine specifications list the fuel rating or grade, and converting away from it of any sort is major.
notes.evidence: (vi) Conversions of any sort for the purpose of using fuel of a rating or grade other than that listed in the engine specifications.

notes.front: When are the changes listed in appendix A(a)(3) propeller major alterations?
notes.back: When they are not authorised in the propeller specifications issued by the FAA.
notes.explanation: As with engines, the FAA’s specifications decide whether a listed change is major.
notes.evidence: The following alterations of a propeller when not authorized in the propeller specifications issued by the FAA are propeller major alterations:

notes.front: Which change to the central part of a propeller, not authorised in its specifications, is a propeller major alteration?
notes.back: A change in hub design.
notes.explanation: Hub design sits beside blade design as a listed propeller major alteration.
notes.evidence: (ii) Changes in hub design.

notes.front: Besides blade and hub design, which other design change is a propeller major alteration under appendix A(a)(3)?
notes.back: A change in the governor or control design.
notes.explanation: Changing how the governor or control is designed is listed separately from installing a new governor.
notes.evidence: (iii) Changes in the governor or control design.

notes.front: Which ice-protection installation is a propeller major alteration when not authorised in the propeller specifications?
notes.back: Installation of a propeller de-icing system.
notes.explanation: Adding a de-icing system to a propeller is listed on its own.
notes.evidence: (v) Installation of propeller de-icing system.

notes.front: Which parts installation is a propeller major alteration under appendix A(a)(3)(vi)?
notes.back: Installation of parts not approved for the propeller.
notes.explanation: Fitting unapproved parts closes the list of propeller major alterations.
notes.evidence: (vi) Installation of parts not approved for the propeller.

notes.front: Which supercharger feature makes separating a reciprocating engine’s crankcase or crankshaft a powerplant major repair?
notes.back: An integral supercharger.
notes.explanation: Separation or disassembly of the crankcase or crankshaft is a major repair on engines equipped with an integral supercharger.
notes.evidence: (i) Separation or disassembly of a crankcase or crankshaft of a reciprocating engine equipped with an integral supercharger.

notes.front: Which propeller reduction gearing makes separating a reciprocating engine’s crankcase or crankshaft a powerplant major repair?
notes.back: Any gearing other than spur-type propeller reduction gearing.
notes.explanation: Appendix A names engines with other than spur-type gearing; spur-type gearing is the exception.
notes.evidence: (ii) Separation or disassembly of a crankcase or crankshaft of a reciprocating engine equipped with other than spur-type propeller reduction gearing.

notes.front: Which special repairs to structural engine parts are powerplant major repairs?
notes.back: Special repairs by welding, plating, metallising, or other methods.
notes.explanation: The third powerplant major repair turns on the method used on a structural engine part.
notes.evidence: (iii) Special repairs to structural engine parts by welding, plating, metalizing, or other methods.

notes.front: Which repairs to steel propeller blades are propeller major repairs?
notes.back: Any repairs to, or straightening of, steel blades.
notes.explanation: For steel blades, any repair at all, including straightening, is a propeller major repair.
notes.evidence: (i) Any repairs to, or straightening of steel blades.

notes.front: Which work on steel propeller hubs is a propeller major repair?
notes.back: Repairing or machining of steel hubs.
notes.explanation: Steel hubs appear next to steel blades on the list of propeller major repairs.
notes.evidence: (ii) Repairing or machining of steel hubs.

notes.front: Which change to blade length is a propeller major repair?
notes.back: Shortening of blades.
notes.explanation: Shortening blades is listed as a propeller major repair whatever the blade material.
notes.evidence: (iii) Shortening of blades.

notes.front: Which lamination work on fixed pitch wood propellers is a propeller major repair?
notes.back: Replacement of outer laminations.
notes.explanation: The list names outer laminations on fixed pitch wood propellers specifically.
notes.evidence: (v) Replacement of outer laminations on fixed pitch wood propellers.

notes.front: Which hub repair on fixed pitch wood propellers is a propeller major repair?
notes.back: Repairing elongated bolt holes in the hub.
notes.explanation: Elongated hub bolt holes on fixed pitch wood propellers are listed on their own.
notes.evidence: (vi) Repairing elongated bolt holes in the hub of fixed pitch wood propellers.

notes.front: Besides retipping and outer laminations, which other work on wood blades is a propeller major repair?
notes.back: Inlay work on wood blades.
notes.explanation: Inlay work completes the wood-blade items on the list.
notes.evidence: (vii) Inlay work on wood blades.

notes.front: Which repairs to composition propeller blades are propeller major repairs?
notes.back: Repairs to composition blades.
notes.explanation: Composition blades are listed without qualification, so their repairs are major.
notes.evidence: (viii) Repairs to composition blades.

notes.front: Which fabric work on a propeller is a propeller major repair?
notes.back: Replacement of tip fabric.
notes.explanation: Replacing tip fabric is listed as a propeller major repair.
notes.evidence: (ix) Replacement of tip fabric.

notes.front: Which covering work on a propeller is a propeller major repair?
notes.back: Replacement of plastic covering.
notes.explanation: Replacing plastic covering sits beside tip fabric on the list.
notes.evidence: (x) Replacement of plastic covering.

notes.front: Which repair to a propeller’s speed-control unit is a propeller major repair?
notes.back: Repair of propeller governors.
notes.explanation: Governor repair is listed, as governor installation is among the alterations.
notes.evidence: (xi) Repair of propeller governors.

notes.front: Which overhaul is listed as a propeller major repair?
notes.back: Overhaul of controllable pitch propellers.
notes.explanation: Appendix A lists the overhaul of controllable pitch propellers as a major repair.
notes.evidence: (xii) Overhaul of controllable pitch propellers.

notes.front: Which work on aluminium propeller blades is a propeller major repair?
notes.back: Repairs to deep dents, cuts, scars, nicks, etc., and straightening of aluminium blades.
notes.explanation: For aluminium blades the list names deep damage and straightening.
notes.evidence: (xiii) Repairs to deep dents, cuts, scars, nicks, etc., and straightening of aluminum blades.

notes.front: Which work inside propeller blades is a propeller major repair?
notes.back: The repair or replacement of internal elements of blades.
notes.explanation: Internal blade elements close the list of propeller major repairs.
notes.evidence: (xiv) The repair or replacement of internal elements of blades.

notes.front: Under 43.2(a)(1), an engine may be described as overhauled only if it has been disassembled, cleaned, inspected, {{c1::repaired as necessary}}, and reassembled, using methods acceptable to the Administrator.
notes.back: repaired as necessary
notes.explanation: The steps must be done with methods, techniques and practices acceptable to the Administrator before the word overhauled may be used.
notes.evidence: (1) Using methods, techniques, and practices acceptable to the Administrator, it has been disassembled, cleaned, inspected, repaired as necessary, and reassembled; and

notes.front: Under 43.2(b), to what standard must an engine described as rebuilt have been tested, and with which parts?
notes.back: To the same tolerances and limits as a new item, using new parts or used parts within new-part limits or approved oversize or undersize dimensions.
notes.explanation: Even used parts must meet new-part tolerances and limits or approved oversize or undersize dimensions.
notes.evidence: reassembled, and tested to the same tolerances and limits as a new item, using either new parts or used parts that either conform to new part tolerances and limits or to approved oversized or undersized dimensions.

notes.front: Besides the 43.9(a) record entry, what does 43.9(d) require for a powerplant major repair or major alteration?
notes.back: Entry on a form, disposed of as appendix B prescribes, by the person performing the work.
notes.explanation: Major repairs and alterations need both the ordinary entry and the form.
notes.evidence: In addition to the entry required by paragraph (a) of this section, major repairs and major alterations shall be entered on a form, and the form disposed of, in the manner prescribed in appendix B, by the person performing the work.

notes.front: How does 43.10 define life status?
notes.back: The accumulated cycles, hours, or any other mandatory replacement limit of a life-limited part.
notes.explanation: Life status is what every 43.10 control method has to record or show.
notes.evidence: Life status means the accumulated cycles, hours, or any other mandatory replacement limit of a life-limited part.

notes.front: When does a life-limited part removed temporarily for maintenance need no 43.10(c) disposition?
notes.back: When its life status has not changed, it goes back on the same serial-numbered product, and that product accumulates no time in service meanwhile.
notes.explanation: All three conditions must hold; otherwise one of the 43.10(c) control methods applies.
notes.evidence: (1) The life status of the part has not changed; (2) The removal and reinstallation is performed on the same serial numbered product; and (3) That product does not accumulate time in service while the part is removed.

notes.front: What must any control method for a removed life-limited part achieve under 43.10(c)?
notes.back: It must deter installation of the part after it has reached its life limit.
notes.explanation: The listed methods are all ways of meeting this one aim.
notes.evidence: The method must deter the installation of the part after it has reached its life limit.

notes.front: Which 43.10(c) method controls a removed life-limited part through a system that substantiates its part number, serial number and current life status?
notes.back: A record keeping system (electronic, paper or other means).
notes.explanation: The record must be updated with the current life status each time the part is removed.
notes.evidence: The part may be controlled using a record keeping system that substantiates the part number, serial number, and current life status of the part. Each time the part is removed from a type certificated product, the record must be updated with the current life status.

notes.front: Under 43.10(c)(2), what must a tag attached to a removed life-limited part include?
notes.back: The part number, serial number and current life status.
notes.explanation: At each removal a new tag is made or the existing one updated with the current life status.
notes.evidence: The tag or record must include the part number, serial number, and current life status of the part. Each time the part is removed from a type certificated product, either a new tag or record must be created, or the existing tag or record must be updated with the current life status.

notes.front: Under 43.10(c)(3), what may be done if a non-permanent life-status mark is removed?
notes.back: Another method in 43.10 may be used.
notes.explanation: A non-permanent mark must be updated at each removal, and losing it lets the owner switch to another method.
notes.evidence: The life status must be updated each time the part is removed from a type certificated product, or if the mark is removed, another method in this section may be used.

notes.front: Under 43.10(c)(4), when may a permanent life-status mark be made without following the 45.16 instructions?
notes.back: When the part is permanently removed from use on type-certificated products.
notes.explanation: Otherwise the permanent mark must follow 45.16 to maintain the integrity of the part.
notes.evidence: Unless the part is permanently removed from use on type certificated products, this permanent mark must be accomplished in accordance with the instructions under § 45.16 of this chapter in order to maintain the integrity of the part.

notes.front: Under 43.10(c)(5), what must segregation of a life-limited part include, at least?
notes.back: A record of part number, serial number and current life status, and physical storage apart from parts eligible for installation.
notes.explanation: Segregation combines a record with physical separation, both aimed at deterring installation.
notes.evidence: (i) Maintaining a record of the part number, serial number, and current life status, and (ii) Ensuring the part is physically stored separately from parts that are currently eligible for installation.

notes.front: What standard must mutilation of a life-limited part meet under 43.10(c)(6)?
notes.back: It must render the part beyond repair and incapable of being reworked to appear airworthy.
notes.explanation: Mutilation deters installation by making the part impossible to rework into something that looks airworthy.
notes.evidence: The mutilation must render the part beyond repair and incapable of being reworked to appear to be airworthy.

notes.front: Besides the six named methods, what other control method does 43.10(c) accept?
notes.back: Any other method approved or accepted by the FAA.
notes.explanation: The named methods are listed as acceptable methods, and the list is left open for FAA-approved or accepted alternatives.
notes.evidence: (7) Other methods. Any other method approved or accepted by the FAA.

notes.front: When a removed life-limited part is sold, what must go with it under 43.10(d)?
notes.back: The mark, tag or other record used to comply with 43.10, unless the part was mutilated first.
notes.explanation: The record travels with the part so the next owner knows its life status.
notes.evidence: must transfer with the part the mark, tag, or other record used to comply with this section, unless the part is mutilated before it is sold or transferred.

notes.front: In what does 33.70 require the operating limitations of each engine life-limited part to be expressed?
notes.back: The maximum allowable number of flight cycles.
notes.explanation: The limit is set by an FAA-approved procedure and counted in flight cycles, not hours.
notes.evidence: By a procedure approved by the FAA, operating limitations must be established which specify the maximum allowable number of flight cycles for each engine life-limited part.

notes.front: What are two parts that 33.70 says typically are engine life-limited parts?
notes.back: Disks and shafts (the list, which is not exhaustive, also includes spacers, hubs, high-pressure casings and non-redundant mount components).
notes.explanation: The rule gives these as typical examples and says the list is not limited to them.
notes.evidence: Typically, engine life-limited parts include, but are not limited to disks, spacers, hubs, shafts, high-pressure casings, and non-redundant mount components.

notes.front: Under 33.70(a), what must the engineering plan ensure for each engine life-limited part?
notes.back: That it is withdrawn from service at an approved life before hazardous engine effects can occur.
notes.explanation: The engineering plan is the first of the three plans the applicant uses to establish each part’s integrity.
notes.evidence: (a) An engineering plan that contains the steps required to ensure each engine life-limited part is withdrawn from service at an approved life before hazardous engine effects can occur.

notes.front: What does the 33.70(b) manufacturing plan identify?
notes.back: The manufacturing constraints needed to produce each engine life-limited part consistently with the attributes the engineering plan requires.
notes.explanation: It links how the part is made to what the engineering plan assumes.
notes.evidence: (b) A manufacturing plan that identifies the specific manufacturing constraints necessary to consistently produce each engine life-limited part with the attributes required by the engineering plan.

notes.front: What does the 33.70(c) service management plan define, and where do its processes end up?
notes.back: In-service maintenance processes and repair limitations for each part; they become part of the Instructions for Continued Airworthiness.
notes.explanation: This is the plan that reaches mechanics, through the ICA.
notes.evidence: (c) A service management plan that defines in-service processes for maintenance and the limitations to repair for each engine life-limited part that will maintain attributes consistent with those required by the engineering plan. These processes and limitations will become part of the Instructions for Continued Airworthiness.

notes.front: Where must an engine applicant publish the list of engine life-limited parts and the approved life of each?
notes.back: In the Airworthiness Limitations Section of the Instructions for Continued Airworthiness.
notes.explanation: Section 33.70 ties the approved lives to the ICA required by 33.4.
notes.evidence: Applicants must publish a list of the life-limited engine parts and the approved life for each part in the Airworthiness Limitations Section of the Instructions for Continued Airworthiness as required by § 33.4 of this part.

notes.front: Under 33.4, when may an engine’s Instructions for Continued Airworthiness be incomplete at type certification?
notes.back: When a program exists to complete them before the first aircraft with the engine is delivered or gets its standard airworthiness certificate, whichever is later.
notes.explanation: Completion may follow type certification only under such a program.
notes.evidence: The instructions may be incomplete at type certification if a program exists to ensure their completion prior to delivery of the first aircraft with the engine installed, or upon issuance of a standard certificate of airworthiness for the aircraft with the engine installed, whichever occurs later.

notes.front: How must the Airworthiness Limitations section appear in an engine’s ICA under appendix A to part 33?
notes.back: As a section titled Airworthiness Limitations, segregated and clearly distinguishable from the rest of the manual.
notes.explanation: It must be clearly distinguishable from the rest of the manual, not buried within it.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 33, appendix A, A33.4 (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition), PDF p. 44
notes.evidence: The Instructions for Continued Airworthiness must contain a section titled Airworthiness Limitations that is segregated and clearly distinguishable from the rest of the manual.

notes.front: What must an engine’s Airworthiness Limitations section set forth?
notes.back: Each mandatory replacement time, inspection interval, and related procedure required for type certification.
notes.explanation: If the ICA runs to several documents, this section must be in the principal manual.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 33, appendix A, A33.4(a)(1) (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition), PDF p. 44
notes.evidence: The Airworthiness Limitations section must set forth each mandatory replacement time, inspection interval, and related procedure required for type certification. If the Instructions for Continued Airworthiness consist of multiple documents, the section required under this paragraph must be included in the principal manual.

notes.front: Under which two sections does the required statement in an engine’s Airworthiness Limitations section say it specifies maintenance?
notes.back: Sections 43.16 and 91.403, unless an alternative program has been FAA approved.
notes.explanation: The statement ties the section to the mechanic’s rule (43.16) and the operator’s rule (91.403).
notes.source: 14 CFR part 33, appendix A, A33.4(a)(2) (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition), PDF p. 44
notes.evidence: The Airworthiness Limitations section is FAA approved and specifies maintenance required under §§ 43.16 and 91.403 of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations unless an alternative program has been FAA approved.

notes.front: What must the scheduling information in an engine maintenance manual also include, under appendix A to part 33?
notes.back: The recommended overhaul periods and cross references to the Airworthiness Limitations section.
notes.explanation: Recommended overhaul periods sit in the scheduling information, alongside references to the mandatory section.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 33, appendix A, A33.3(a)(6) (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition), PDF p. 43
notes.evidence: The recommended overhaul periods and necessary cross references to the Airworthiness Limitations section of the manual must also be included.

notes.front: Under 33.7(a), where are an engine’s ratings and operating limitations included?
notes.back: In the engine certificate data sheet specified in 21.41, as established by the Administrator.
notes.explanation: The Administrator establishes them and records them in the engine certificate data sheet.
notes.evidence: Engine ratings and operating limitations are established by the Administrator and included in the engine certificate data sheet specified in § 21.41 of this chapter

notes.front: What are two grades or specifications that 33.7(b) sets as operating limitations for reciprocating engines?
notes.back: Fuel grade or specification, and oil grade or specification.
notes.explanation: Both appear among the reciprocating-engine ratings and limitations, alongside temperatures and pressures.
notes.evidence: (2) Fuel grade or specification. (3) Oil grade or specification.

notes.front: Under 91.417(a)(2), which overhaul-related time must the owner record for items overhauled on a specified time basis?
notes.back: The time since last overhaul of all such items installed on the aircraft.
notes.explanation: It applies to items required to be overhauled on a specified time basis.
notes.evidence: The time since last overhaul of all items installed on the aircraft which are required to be overhauled on a specified time basis.

notes.front: Under 91.421(a), what maintenance record may an owner use for an engine rebuilt by the manufacturer?
notes.back: A new maintenance record, without previous operating history.
notes.explanation: This is what is meant by a zero-time engine.
notes.evidence: The owner or operator may use a new maintenance record, without previous operating history, for an aircraft engine rebuilt by the manufacturer or by an agency approved by the manufacturer.

notes.front: What must the manufacturer or agency enter in the new record of a zero-timed rebuilt engine?
notes.back: A signed statement of the rebuild date, each change required by ADs, and each SB change if the bulletin requests the entry.
notes.explanation: Although history is wiped, AD changes and requested SB changes must still be traceable.
notes.evidence: (1) A signed statement of the date the engine was rebuilt; (2) Each change made as required by airworthiness directives; and (3) Each change made in compliance with manufacturer's service bulletins, if the entry is specifically requested in that bulletin.

notes.front: Under 91.421(c), what must every part used in a rebuilt engine conform to?
notes.back: The production drawing tolerances and limits for new parts, or approved oversize or undersize dimensions for a new engine.
notes.explanation: Used parts are allowed, but only within new-part limits or approved oversize or undersize dimensions.
notes.evidence: However, all parts used in it must conform to the production drawing tolerances and limits for new parts or be of approved oversized or undersized dimensions for a new engine.

notes.front: Under 91.403(c), what must have been complied with before an aircraft whose manual or ICA has an airworthiness limitations section is operated?
notes.back: The mandatory replacement times, inspection intervals and related procedures in that section, or approved alternatives.
notes.explanation: Alternatives must come from approved part 121 or 135 operations specifications or a 91.409(e) inspection program.
notes.evidence: unless the mandatory replacement times, inspection intervals, and related procedures specified in that section or alternative inspection intervals and related procedures set forth in an operations specification approved by the Administrator under part 121 or 135 of this chapter or in accordance with an inspection program approved under § 91.409(e) have been complied with.

notes.front: Under 43.16, how must a mechanic perform an inspection or other maintenance specified in an Airworthiness Limitations section?
notes.back: In accordance with that section, or approved part 121 or 135 operations specifications, or a 91.409(e) inspection program.
notes.explanation: The mechanic’s rule mirrors the operator’s rule in 91.403(c).
notes.evidence: shall perform the inspection or other maintenance in accordance with that section, or in accordance with operations specifications approved by the Administrator under part 121 or 135, or an inspection program approved under § 91.409(e).

notes.front: What does the handbook call the final authority in deciding whether an engine must be replaced?
notes.back: The applicable manufacturer’s instructions.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives the common reasons for removal, but in every case defers to the manufacturer’s instructions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reasons for Removal of Reciprocating Engines”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: in every case, consult applicable manufacturer’s instructions as the final authority in establishing the basis for engine replacement.

notes.front: What is sudden stoppage of an engine?
notes.back: A very rapid and complete stoppage in which rpm goes to zero in less than one complete propeller revolution.
notes.explanation: It can come from engine seizure or from a blade striking an object.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-2b, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: Sudden stoppage is a very rapid and complete stoppage of the engine. It can be caused by engine seizure or by one or more of the propeller blades striking an object in such a way that rpm goes to zero in less than one complete revolution of the propeller.

notes.front: What is a sudden reduction in engine speed?
notes.back: A blade strikes an object at low rpm; the object is cleared and the engine recovers rpm and keeps running.
notes.explanation: Unlike sudden stoppage, the engine keeps turning unless it is stopped to prevent further damage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Sudden Reduction in Speed”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: Sudden reduction in engine speed can occur when one or more of the propeller blades strike an object at a low engine rpm. After impact, the foreign object is cleared and the engine recovers rpm and continues to run unless stopped to prevent further damage.

notes.front: After a sudden reduction in speed, what must follow if the external inspection finds damage that line maintenance cannot correct?
notes.back: Remove the engine.
notes.explanation: The first step is an external look at the engine mount, crankcase and nose section.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Sudden Reduction in Speed”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: Make a thorough external inspection of the engine mount, crankcase, and nose section to determine whether any parts have been damaged. If damage is found that cannot be corrected by line maintenance, remove the engine.

notes.front: Which engine operational problem does the handbook say is especially true of turbine engines?
notes.back: Excessive engine vibration.
notes.explanation: It is the first item in the handbook’s list of engine operational problems.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Operational Problems”, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: Excessive engine vibration; this is especially true with turbine engines.

notes.front: In the handbook’s list of engine operational problems, what generally causes low power output in reciprocating engines?
notes.back: Low compression.
notes.explanation: For turbines the handbook blames internal deterioration or damage instead.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Operational Problems”, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: Low power output, generally caused by low compression, with reciprocating engines and internal engine deterioration or damage with turbines.

notes.front: What are two factors on which the handbook says engine life depends?
notes.back: Operational use and the quality of manufacture or overhaul (also aircraft type, kind of operation, degree of maintenance).
notes.explanation: Because life depends on so many factors, the manufacturer sets the removal times.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine or Component Lifespan Exceeded”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: Engine life is dependent upon such factors as operational use, the quality of manufacture or overhaul, the type of aircraft in which the engine is installed, the kind of operation being carried out, and the degree to which maintenance is accomplished. Thus, the manufacturer sets engine removal times.

notes.front: Why may turbine blades, turbine discs or combustion liners have shorter life limits than the engine?
notes.back: Because of the stresses imposed on those parts during operation.
notes.explanation: The manufacturer sets these shorter limits for critical turbine components.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine or Component Lifespan Exceeded”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: Certain critical components of turbine engines such as turbine blades, turbine discs or combustion liners may have shorter life limits established by the manufacturer due to the stresses imposed on those parts during operation.

notes.front: What does the FAA require of the engine manufacturer about mandatory replacement times?
notes.back: That the manufacturer identify and establish which parts have mandatory replacement times.
notes.explanation: This links the handbook’s removal reasons to the regulatory life limits.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine or Component Lifespan Exceeded”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: The FAA requires that the manufacture identify and establish which parts have mandatory replacement times.

notes.front: What do heavy metal particles in the drained and strained engine oil indicate?
notes.back: A definite engine failure; the engine must be removed.
notes.explanation: The handbook separates heavy particles, which mean removal, from fine filings, which mean further inspection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Sudden Reduction in Speed”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: Heavy metal particles in the oil indicate a definite engine failure, and the engine must be removed.

notes.front: Before removing an engine for suspected internal failure, how do you tell whether screen particles are ferrous metal?
notes.back: Place them close to a magnet to see if they are magnetic.
notes.explanation: The magnet shows whether the particles are ferrous before removal is decided.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Metal Particles in the Oil”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: determine if the foreign particles are ferrous metal by placing them close to a magnet to see if they are magnetic.

notes.front: Why might particles on oil screens or magnetic chip detectors not be metal at all?
notes.back: Carbon breaks loose inside the engine in rock-like pieces that look like metal.
notes.explanation: The handbook says to consider this possibility when foreign particles are found.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Metal Particles in the Oil”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: Carbon tends to break loose from the interior of the engine in rock-like pieces that have the appearance of metal.

notes.front: In what unit do oil analysis programs measure wear-metal particles?
notes.back: Parts per million, by weight.
notes.explanation: The programs both identify and measure the particles, in parts per million by weight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spectrometric Oil Analysis Engine Inspection Program”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: Oil analysis programs identify and measure these particles in parts per million (PPM) by weight.

notes.front: What are two advantages of oil analysis that the handbook gives?
notes.back: Increased safety, by noticing a problem before engine failure; and saving money, by finding problems before they grow.
notes.explanation: Both come from catching the problem early.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spectrometric Oil Analysis Engine Inspection Program”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: The advantage of oil analysis is an increase in safety by noticing an engine problem before engine failure. It also saves money by finding engine problems before they become large problems or complete engine failure.

notes.front: Before starting work to remove a reciprocating engine, why confirm the magneto switch is off?
notes.back: The engine can be started accidentally by turning the propeller if the magneto switch is on.
notes.explanation: This is the handbook’s first step in preparing the engine for removal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Preparing the Engine for Removal”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: Before starting to work on the aircraft or reciprocating engine, always be sure that the magneto switch is in the off position. Aircraft engines can be started accidentally by turning the propeller if the magneto switch is on.

notes.front: Before lifting an engine, what does the handbook say to check about the sling, the hoist and the engine?
notes.back: Inspect the sling’s condition, make sure the hoist has sufficient capacity, and take the engine’s centre of gravity into account.
notes.explanation: The handbook presents these as safety checks before the engine’s weight is taken.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Removing the Engine”, p. 8-9
notes.evidence: As a matter of safety, carefully inspect the sling for condition before installing it on the engine. Before attaching the sling to the hoist, be sure that the hoist has sufficient capacity to lift the engine safely. The engine’s center of gravity (CG) should also be taken into account as the engine is hoisted.

notes.front: After an engine is mounted and the nuts safetied, what is connected across each engine mount?
notes.back: Bonding strips, to provide an electrical path from the mount to the airframe.
notes.explanation: The handbook fits them once the sling and hoist are removed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Hoisting & Mounting the Engine for Installation”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: After the nuts are safetied and the engine sling and hoist are removed, bonding strips should be connected across each engine mount to provide an electrical path from the mount to the airframe.

notes.front: When an engine is changed because of internal failure, why must some accessories be replaced regardless of operating time?
notes.back: They may have been contaminated by metal particles carried in by the engine oil that lubricates them.
notes.explanation: Internal failure spreads metal through the oil to accessories lubricated by it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Inspection & Depreservation of Accessories”, p. 8-5
notes.evidence: Some accessories must be replaced, regardless of their operating time, if the engine is being changed because of internal failure. Such accessories may have been contaminated by metal particles carried into their operating mechanisms by the engine oil that lubricates them.

notes.front: During an engine change, how are the engine mounting frame and its mounting bolts inspected?
notes.back: Frame: for distortion such as bends, dents, flat spots, corrosion or cracks (dye penetrant for cracks). Bolts: usually by magnetic particle inspection.
notes.explanation: Dye penetrant reveals cracks, porous areas or other defects in the tubing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Inspection & Replacement of Powerplant External Units & Systems”, p. 8-5
notes.evidence: The engine mounting frame assembly should be checked for any distortion of the steel tubing, such as bends, dents, flat spots, corrosion, or cracks. Use the dye penetrant inspection method to reveal a crack, porous area, or other defects. The engine mounting bolts are usually checked for condition by magnetic particle inspection or other approved processes.

notes.front: Why should a newly installed engine be pre-oiled before its initial start?
notes.back: To prevent failure of the engine bearings during the initial start.
notes.explanation: After a long idle period, bearing surfaces are likely to be dry where the corrosion-preventive mixture has dried out or drained away.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pre-Oiling”, p. 8-12
notes.evidence: To prevent failure of the engine bearings during the initial start, the engine should be pre-oiled. When an engine has been idle for an extended period of time, its internal bearing surfaces are likely to become dry at points where the corrosion-preventive mixture has dried out or drained away from the bearings.

notes.front: Within how long of pre-oiling should an engine generally be operated?
notes.back: Within 4 hours; otherwise the pre-oiling procedure normally must be repeated.
notes.explanation: The handbook states this as a general limit, not a fixed rule.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pre-Oiling”, p. 8-13
notes.evidence: Generally, the engine should be operated within 4 hours of being pre-oiled; otherwise, the pre-oiling procedure normally must be repeated.

notes.front: When rigging a reciprocating engine throttle, adjust the control so that it has a slight {{c1::cushion}} action at the full-open and idle positions on the throttle quadrant.
notes.back: cushion
notes.explanation: The cushion is set at both ends of throttle valve travel, stop to stop.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Connections & Adjustments”, p. 8-11
notes.evidence: adjust the throttle control so that it has a slight cushion action at two positions on the throttle quadrant: one when the carburetor throttle valve is in the full-open position and the other when it is closed to the idle position (stop to stop).

notes.front: What does the cushion in a rigged throttle control ensure?
notes.back: That the throttle valve’s travel is not limited by the quadrant stops, so it opens fully and closes to the correct idle.
notes.explanation: The idle position is then set by the throttle arm stop, not by the quadrant.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Connections & Adjustments”, p. 8-12
notes.evidence: The presence of this cushion ensures that the travel of the throttle valve is not limited by the stops on the throttle control quadrant, but that they are opening fully and closing to the correct idle speed as determined by the throttle arm stop.

notes.front: What is the engine mount ring?
notes.back: The section of an engine mount where the engine is attached, usually steel tubing of larger diameter, circular to surround the engine.
notes.explanation: The ring surrounds the engine near its point of balance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Turbine Vibration Isolation Engine Mounts”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: The section of an engine mount where the engine is attached is known as the engine mount ring. It is usually constructed of steel tubing having a larger diameter than the rest of the mount structure. It is circular in shape so that it can surround the engine, which is near the point of balance for the engine.

notes.front: Which loads do the forward turbine vibration isolator mounts carry?
notes.back: Vertical, side and axial (thrust) loads, while allowing engine growth from thermal expansion.
notes.explanation: The forward mounts are the ones that take thrust.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Turbine Vibration Isolation Engine Mounts”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: The forward vibration isolator engine mounts carry vertical, side, and axial (thrust) loads and allow engine growth due to thermal expansion.

notes.front: In AC 43.13-1B’s engine-mount inspection, what is the engine-mount structure inspected for, and what happens to the mount bolts?
notes.back: Bent, cracked or buckled tubes; the engine-mount bolts and mount hold-down bolts are removed and replaced.
notes.explanation: The AC also checks the adjacent firewall structure for cracks, distortion or wrinkles.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-2f, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: (2) Inspect the engine-mount structure for bent, cracked, or buckled tubes. (3) Check the adjacent airframe structure firewall for cracks, distortion, or wrinkles. (4) Remove engine-mount bolts and mount hold-down bolts and replace.

notes.front: What is the purpose of testing cylinder compression?
notes.back: To determine whether cylinder replacement is necessary.
notes.explanation: Finding and replacing defective cylinders prevents a complete engine change because of cylinder failure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Compression Tests”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: The purpose of testing cylinder compression is to determine whether cylinder replacement is necessary. The detection and replacement of defective cylinders prevents a complete engine change because of cylinder failure.

notes.front: To what can low compression, for the most part, be traced?
notes.back: Leaky valves.
notes.explanation: Valves are the usual culprit, though not the only one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Compression Tests”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: Low compression, for the most part, can be traced to leaky valves.

notes.front: What are two valve-related conditions that affect engine compression?
notes.back: Incorrect valve clearances; burned or warped valves (also carbon between valve face and seat, and early or late valve timing).
notes.explanation: Four of the six listed conditions involve the valves or their timing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Compression Tests”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: 1. Incorrect valve clearances. 2. Worn, scuffed, or damaged piston. 3. Excessive wear of piston rings and cylinder walls. 4. Burned or warped valves. 5. Carbon particles between the face and the seat of the valve or valves. 6. Early or late valve timing.

notes.front: What are two piston-related conditions that affect engine compression?
notes.back: A worn, scuffed or damaged piston; and excessive wear of piston rings and cylinder walls.
notes.explanation: They are the two listed conditions that concern the piston, rings and cylinder walls.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Compression Tests”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: 2. Worn, scuffed, or damaged piston. 3. Excessive wear of piston rings and cylinder walls.

notes.front: On what principle does the differential pressure tester operate?
notes.back: For any given airflow through a fixed orifice, a constant pressure drop across the orifice results.
notes.explanation: The tester reads leakage by the pressure drop across a fixed orifice.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Differential Pressure Tester”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: The operation of the compression tester is based on the principle that, for any given airflow through a fixed orifice, a constant pressure drop across the orifice results.

notes.front: To what regulated pressure is a differential compression tester set, with air flowing into the cylinder?
notes.back: 80 psi.
notes.explanation: If the regulated pressure is more or less than 80 psi, the regulator is readjusted.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Differential Pressure Tester”, p. 10-40
notes.evidence: re-check the regulated pressure to see that it is 80 psi with air flowing into the cylinder. If the regulated pressure is more or less than 80 psi, readjust the regulator in the test unit to obtain 80 psi.

notes.front: Where must the piston be when air pressure is applied in a differential compression test?
notes.back: At top centre on the compression stroke.
notes.explanation: Air is applied only with the piston at top centre of the compression stroke.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Differential Pressure Tester”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: The differential pressure tester requires the application of air pressure to the cylinder being tested with the piston at top-center compression stroke.

notes.front: If low compression is not cured by re-running and is not due to valve clearance, what does the handbook describe next, with the manufacturer’s approval?
notes.back: Tap a fibre drift on the rocker arm over the valve stem to dislodge foreign material, rotate the engine to reseat the valve, then recheck.
notes.explanation: The handbook says this staking should only be done if the manufacturer approves it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Differential Pressure Tester”, p. 10-40
notes.evidence: place a fiber drift on the rocker arm immediately over the valve stem and tap the drift several times with a 1 to 2 pound hammer to dislodge any foreign material that may be lodged between the valve and valve seat.

notes.front: How do you check whether leakage past the piston is caused by lack of oil?
notes.back: Apply engine oil into the cylinder and around the piston, then recheck; if compression reaches the minimum, keep the cylinder in service.
notes.explanation: A lack of oil can cause this leakage, so adding oil tests that explanation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Differential Pressure Tester”, p. 10-41
notes.evidence: This leakage may occur because of lack of oil. To check this possibility, apply engine oil into the cylinder and around the piston. Then, re-check the compression. If this procedure raises compression to or above the minimum required, continue the cylinder in service.

notes.front: Under AC 43.13-1B, what reading on a hot engine, not raised by the corrective steps, means the cylinder must be removed and inspected?
notes.back: Less than 60/80 on the differential test gauges.
notes.explanation: Removal follows only when the recheck and valve-seating steps in 8-14b(5)(i) and (j) fail to raise the reading.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-14, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: If a cylinder has less than a 60/80 reading on the differential test gauges on a hot engine and procedures in subparagraphs 8-14b(5)(i) and (j) fail to raise the compression reading, the cylinder must be removed and inspected.

notes.front: In AC 43.13-1B’s differential test, what leakage is cause to suspect a cylinder is defective?
notes.back: A loss in excess of 25 percent of the input air pressure.
notes.explanation: The loss is the difference between the cylinder gauge and the regulator gauge.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-14b(5)(i), p. 8-10
notes.evidence: The difference between this pressure and the pressure shown by the regulator pressure gauge is the amount of leakage through the cylinder. A loss in excess of 25 percent of the input air pressure is cause to suspect the cylinder of being defective;

notes.front: After a first suspect reading, how long does AC 43.13-1B say to operate the engine before rechecking?
notes.back: At least 3 minutes, to allow the rings to seal with oil.
notes.explanation: The AC treats a first reading as suspicion, not proof, until this recheck.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-14b(5)(i), p. 8-10
notes.evidence: however, recheck the readings after operating the engine for at least 3 minutes to allow for sealing of the rings with oil.

notes.front: During a compression check, where do you listen for leakage past the exhaust valve?
notes.back: At the exhaust outlet.
notes.explanation: Each leak path vents at a different place, which is how the source is found.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Differential Pressure Tester”, p. 10-40
notes.evidence: At the exhaust valve by listening for air leakage at the exhaust outlet;

notes.front: During a compression check, where does air escape if the intake valve is leaking?
notes.back: At the air intake.
notes.explanation: The air intake is where intake-valve leakage is heard.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Differential Pressure Tester”, p. 10-40
notes.evidence: At the intake valve by escaping air at the air intake; and

notes.front: In AC 43.13-1B, what does air rushing out of the oil dipstick opening during a compression test show?
notes.back: The piston rings are defective.
notes.explanation: The AC checks for this with the dipstick removed.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-14, p. 8-8
notes.evidence: With the oil dipstick removed, and air is rushing out, the piston rings are defective.

notes.front: When closing the tester’s shutoff valve during a differential test, why must the propeller path be clear?
notes.back: Air pressure in the combustion chamber can rotate the propeller if the piston is not on top dead centre.
notes.explanation: Clearing the propeller path guards against that rotation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Differential Pressure Tester”, p. 10-40
notes.evidence: When closing the shutoff valve, make sure that the propeller path is clear of all objects. There is sufficient air pressure in the combustion chamber to rotate the propeller if the piston is not on top dead center.

notes.front: Before a compression test, why must the ignition switch be off?
notes.back: So that there is no accidental firing of the engine.
notes.explanation: Accidental firing is the risk the handbook names.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Compression Tests”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: Be sure that the ignition switch is in the OFF position so that there is no accidental firing of the engine.

notes.front: Under AC 43.13-1B, what must happen to every engine that suffers a sudden stoppage before it returns to service?
notes.back: It must be inspected in accordance with the manufacturer’s maintenance instructions.
notes.explanation: The manufacturer’s instructions come first; the AC gives a fallback when there are none.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-2b, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: (1) Every engine that suffers a sudden stoppage must be inspected in accordance with the manufacturer’s maintenance instructions before being returned to service.

notes.front: If the engine manufacturer gives no sudden-stoppage information, what does AC 43.13-1B require?
notes.back: Open the engine case and inspect every major component part by visual and/or nondestructive inspection, as applicable.
notes.explanation: Without manufacturer data the AC requires a full internal inspection.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-2b, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: (2) If the engine manufacturer does not provide the required information, then the engine case must be opened, and every major component part must be inspected using visual and/or nondestructive inspection (NDI) procedures as applicable.

notes.front: After a sudden stoppage, what must be checked on the firewall, and where must the damaged propeller go?
notes.back: Firewall: distortion, cracks and elongated bolt holes. Propeller: to an FAA-certificated repair station for complete nondestructive inspection and repair.
notes.explanation: The inspection reaches beyond the engine to the structure and propeller that shared the shock.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-2b(3), p. 8-2
notes.evidence: The aircraft’s firewall must also be checked for distortion, cracks, and elongated bolt holes. The damaged propeller must be sent to a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)-certificated repair station for complete NDI and repair.

notes.front: Besides the engine itself, what do sudden-stoppage inspections include checking, per AC 43.13-1B?
notes.back: Cowling, spinner and airframe cracks and hidden damage, and alignment of the engine mount to the airframe.
notes.explanation: The AC continues with the mounting hardware, isolation mounts and bushings.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-2b(3), p. 8-1
notes.evidence: (3) The sudden-stoppage inspections include checking for cowling, spinner, and airframe cracks and hidden damage and alignment of the engine mount to the airframe, the

notes.front: In AC 43.13-1B’s cold cylinder check for a rough-running engine, how is the dead cylinder found?
notes.back: It is colder than the surrounding cylinders; a thermocouple probe, sensitive to small temperature differences, is used.
notes.explanation: A thermocouple probe is sensitive enough to find small temperature differences between cylinders.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-2a, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: The dead cylinder will be colder than the surrounding cylinders and can be quickly determined by using the recommended cold cylinder checks. This should be done using a thermocouple probe, which is very sensitive to small differences in temperature,

notes.front: After grinding, what do engine manufacturers specify for the nitrided crankshafts of most opposed engines?
notes.back: They must be re-nitrided.
notes.explanation: Grinding a nitrided crankshaft is not the end of the job; the manufacturer specifies re-nitriding.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-3, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: Most opposed engines have nitrided crankshafts, and engine manufacturers specify that these crankshafts must be re-nitrided after grinding.

notes.front: When may used engine parts be installed in a certificated engine, per AC 43.13-1B?
notes.back: When the part conforms to new part tolerances or meets the manufacturer’s service limits.
notes.explanation: Either test is enough: new part tolerances or the manufacturer’s service limits.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-4, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: Used engine parts can be installed if that part either conforms to new part tolerances or meets the manufacturer’s service limits.

notes.front: What are two conditions under which AC 43.13-1B allows self-locking nuts on aircraft engines?
notes.back: Their use is specified by the engine manufacturer; and they will not fall inside the engine if they loosen and come off.
notes.explanation: These are two of the AC’s conditions; its list has more.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-9, p. 8-5
notes.evidence: a. When their use is specified by the engine manufacturer in the assembly drawing, parts list, and bills of material. b. When the nuts will not fall inside the engine should they loosen and come off.

notes.front: Why does AC 43.13-1B warn against long ground run-ups with the cowling off?
notes.back: The engine will overheat because cylinder cooling has been disrupted.
notes.explanation: The warning sits in the AC’s paragraph on running in an overhauled engine.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-13, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: NOTE: Do not run up engines on the ground for long periods of time with the cowling off. The engine will overheat because cylinder cooling has been disrupted.

notes.front: A mechanic has found every item satisfactory on a 100-hour inspection of a piston-engine aeroplane. What does 43.15(c)(2) require before he approves it for return to service?
notes.back: A: Run the engine to check power output, magnetos, fuel and oil pressure, and cylinder and oil temperature
notes.explanation: The rule makes an engine run, judged against the manufacturer’s recommendations, a condition of approving a reciprocating-engine aircraft after an annual or 100-hour inspection.
notes.choices:
A) Run the engine to check power output, magnetos, fuel and oil pressure, and cylinder and oil temperature
B) A test flight by a certificated pilot
C) Nothing more: the completed checklist is enough
D) A differential compression test on every cylinder
notes.choicesExplained: C ignores the run the rule requires before approval. B: the rule requires an engine run, not a test flight. D: compression is an appendix D inspection item, not what 43.15(c)(2) requires before approval.
notes.evidence: Each person approving a reciprocating-engine-powered aircraft for return to service after an annual or 100-hour inspection shall, before that approval, run the aircraft engine or engines to determine satisfactory performance in accordance with the manufacturer's recommendations of

notes.front: A mechanic completes a progressive inspection on a turboprop aeroplane. What must she do with the engines before approving it for return to service?
notes.back: Run them to determine satisfactory performance in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommendations.
notes.explanation: For turbine-powered aircraft the run applies after annual, 100-hour and progressive inspections alike.
notes.evidence: Each person approving a turbine-engine-powered aircraft for return to service after an annual, 100-hour, or progressive inspection shall, before that approval, run the aircraft engine or engines to determine satisfactory performance in accordance with the manufacturer's recommendations.

notes.front: A mechanic wants to use a checklist she wrote herself for a 100-hour inspection. Is that allowed, and what must it contain?
notes.back: Yes, it may be her own design, but it must include the scope and detail of the items in appendix D to part 43.
notes.explanation: The rule accepts a checklist of any origin; what it fixes is the content, by reference to appendix D.
notes.evidence: The checklist may be of the person's own design, one provided by the manufacturer of the equipment being inspected or one obtained from another source. This checklist must include the scope and detail of the items contained in appendix D

notes.front: On a 100-hour inspection a mechanic finds an exhaust stack loosely attached at the cylinder. Which appendix D(d) item covers this, and what does that item check?
notes.back: Exhaust stacks: for cracks, defects, and improper attachment.
notes.explanation: Improper attachment is one of the three things appendix D names for exhaust stacks, so the finding falls under that item.
notes.evidence: (8) Exhaust stacks—for cracks, defects, and improper attachment.

notes.front: An annual inspection finds weak compression on one cylinder. What does appendix D(d)(3) then require the internal engine to be inspected for?
notes.back: Improper internal condition and improper internal tolerances.
notes.explanation: Weak compression triggers a deeper look inside the engine rather than ending the check.
notes.evidence: If there is weak cylinder compression, for improper internal condition and improper internal tolerances.

notes.front: On a 100-hour inspection, a propeller bolt is correctly torqued but has no safety wire. Which appendix D(h) item covers this, and what does it check?
notes.back: Bolts: for improper torquing and lack of safetying.
notes.explanation: Appendix D names lack of safetying for propeller bolts, so correct torque alone does not satisfy the item.
notes.evidence: (2) Bolts—for improper torquing and lack of safetying.

notes.front: A shop fits an accessory to an engine although that accessory is not approved for the engine, and the engine specifications do not list it. How does appendix A to part 43 classify the work?
notes.back: D: A powerplant major alteration
notes.explanation: Installing an accessory not approved for the engine is one of the six listed powerplant major alterations.
notes.choices:
A) A propeller major alteration
B) A powerplant major repair
C) Preventive maintenance
D) A powerplant major alteration
notes.choicesExplained: B: the three powerplant major repairs concern crankcase or crankshaft separation and special structural repairs. C: preventive maintenance is simple work, not unapproved installations. A concerns propellers, not engine accessories.
notes.evidence: (iii) Installation of an accessory which is not approved for the engine.

notes.front: An engine is changed to a configuration that appendix A(a)(2) would normally call a powerplant major alteration, but the FAA’s engine specifications list that configuration. How does appendix A(a)(2) treat it?
notes.back: A: It is not a powerplant major alteration under appendix A(a)(2)
notes.explanation: Appendix A(a)(2) applies only to alterations not listed in the engine specifications issued by the FAA.
notes.choices:
A) It is not a powerplant major alteration under appendix A(a)(2)
B) It is still a powerplant major alteration
C) It becomes a powerplant major repair
D) It needs a supplemental type certificate
