notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the qualifier at the head of the list. C: major repairs are a separate list of repairs, not alterations. D: nothing in appendix A(a)(2) calls for a supplemental type certificate here.
notes.evidence: The following alterations of a powerplant when not listed in the engine specifications issued by the FAA, are powerplant major alterations.

notes.front: A propeller’s blades are redesigned without authorisation in the propeller specifications. How does appendix A classify this?
notes.back: A propeller major alteration: a change in blade design.
notes.explanation: Changes in blade design head the list of propeller major alterations.
notes.evidence: (i) Changes in blade design.

notes.front: A feathering system is fitted to a propeller whose specifications do not authorise it. How does appendix A classify the work?
notes.back: A propeller major alteration: installation of a propeller governor or feathering system.
notes.explanation: Installing a governor or feathering system is itself on the list, not only redesigning one.
notes.evidence: (iv) Installation of a propeller governor or feathering system.

notes.front: A shop restores a worn structural engine part by a special plating repair. How does appendix A to part 43 classify the work?
notes.back: A: A powerplant major repair
notes.explanation: Special repairs to structural engine parts by plating are one of the three listed powerplant major repairs.
notes.choices:
A) A powerplant major repair
B) A powerplant major alteration
C) Preventive maintenance
D) Not listed, so a minor repair
notes.choicesExplained: B: it restores the part rather than altering the engine’s design. C: preventive maintenance is simple work without complex assembly. D: plating of a structural engine part is on the list.
notes.evidence: (iii) Special repairs to structural engine parts by welding, plating, metalizing, or other methods.

notes.front: How does appendix A classify retipping a wood propeller?
notes.back: A propeller major repair.
notes.explanation: Retipping of wood propellers is one of the listed propeller major repairs.
notes.evidence: (iv) Retipping of wood propellers.

notes.front: A shop disassembles, cleans, inspects, repairs and reassembles an engine but does not test it. May its maintenance entry describe the engine as overhauled?
notes.back: No. Section 43.2(a)(2) also requires testing to approved, or acceptable current, standards and technical data.
notes.explanation: The data must be approved, or acceptable and developed by the type certificate, supplemental type certificate or part 21 approval holder.
notes.evidence: (2) It has been tested in accordance with approved standards and technical data, or in accordance with current standards and technical data acceptable to the Administrator, which have been developed and documented by the holder of the type certificate, supplemental type certificate, or a material, part, process, or appliance approval under part 21 of this chapter.

notes.front: A mechanic replaces a magneto and signs the 43.9 maintenance record entry. What does that signature approve?
notes.back: Return to service only for the work performed.
notes.explanation: The signature approves only the work performed, not the whole aircraft or engine.
notes.evidence: The signature constitutes the approval for return to service only for the work performed.

notes.front: A mechanic replaces a cylinder during routine maintenance, not during an inspection. Which record entry does 43.9(a) require in the engine’s maintenance record?
notes.back: D: A description of the work (or reference to acceptable data), the completion date, and the approver’s signature, certificate number and kind of certificate
notes.explanation: Section 43.9(a) sets the content of a maintenance entry for work on an engine: what was done, when, and who approved it.
notes.choices:
A) Only an FAA Form 337, since cylinders are major parts
B) No entry, if the owner keeps the shop’s work order
C) A statement that the aircraft was inspected and found airworthy
D) A description of the work (or reference to acceptable data), the completion date, and the approver’s signature, certificate number and kind of certificate
notes.choicesExplained: A: a form is required only for major repairs and alterations, in addition to the entry. C is the wording of an inspection entry under 43.11, not 43.9. B: 43.9(a) requires the entry in the maintenance record of the equipment.
notes.evidence: shall make an entry in the maintenance record of that equipment containing the following information: (1) A description (or reference to data acceptable to the Administrator) of work performed. (2) The date of completion of the work performed.

notes.front: A mechanic removes a turbine disk that has reached its life limit and wants to make sure it can never be reworked to look airworthy. Which 43.10(c) method achieves that?
notes.back: C: Mutilation
notes.explanation: Only mutilation must leave the part beyond repair and incapable of being reworked to appear airworthy.
notes.choices:
A) A non-permanent marking of its life status
B) A tag attached to the disk
C) Mutilation
D) Segregation in a separate store
notes.choicesExplained: A and B record the life status but leave the disk intact. D keeps it apart from eligible parts but does not make it unrepairable.
notes.evidence: The part may be mutilated to deter its installation in a type certificated product. The mutilation must render the part beyond repair and incapable of being reworked to appear to be airworthy.

notes.front: An owner’s engine records list an airworthiness directive only as “complied with”. Under 91.417(a)(2)(v), what should the AD status record show?
notes.back: A: The method of compliance, the AD number and revision date, and for recurring action when the next action is due
notes.explanation: The owner’s record of AD status must identify each AD and how it was met, and track any recurring action.
notes.choices:
A) The method of compliance, the AD number and revision date, and for recurring action when the next action is due
B) Only the date the AD was issued
C) The name of the mechanic’s employer
D) Nothing more, if the AD was a one-time action
notes.choicesExplained: B: the rule asks for the AD number and revision date and the method of compliance, not the issue date. C is not among the listed items. D: the method, number and revision date apply to every AD, recurring or not.
notes.evidence: The current status of applicable airworthiness directives (AD) including, for each, the method of compliance, the AD number and revision date. If the AD involves recurring action, the time and date when the next action is required.

notes.front: An independent shop with no approval from the engine manufacturer rebuilds an engine to new limits. Under 91.421(a), may the owner start a new record without previous operating history?
notes.back: C: No: that record is for engines rebuilt by the manufacturer or an agency it approved
notes.explanation: The new, history-free record depends on who rebuilt the engine, not only on the standard reached.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because the engine meets new limits
B) Yes, if an FAA Form 8130-3 accompanies the engine
C) No: that record is for engines rebuilt by the manufacturer or an agency it approved
D) Only after a 100-hour inspection
notes.choicesExplained: A: meeting new limits is part of the definition, but the rule also names who must do the rebuilding. B and D add conditions that 91.421 does not contain.
notes.evidence: The owner or operator may use a new maintenance record, without previous operating history, for an aircraft engine rebuilt by the manufacturer or by an agency approved by the manufacturer.

notes.front: An engine’s Airworthiness Limitations section sets a cycle limit for a turbine disk. The records show the disk has passed it, but the engine runs perfectly. The owner has no approved alternative program. May the aircraft be operated?
notes.back: A: No: the mandatory replacement time has not been complied with
notes.explanation: Section 91.403(c) bars operation unless the section’s mandatory replacement times have been complied with.
notes.choices:
A) No: the mandatory replacement time has not been complied with
B) Yes, until the next annual inspection
C) Yes, if a mechanic inspects the disk by borescope
D) Yes, while engine performance remains normal
notes.choicesExplained: D: good running does not satisfy a mandatory replacement time. B: the rule sets no grace period until an inspection. C: an inspection is not a substitute for the replacement time.
notes.evidence: No person may operate an aircraft for which a manufacturer's maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness has been issued that contains an airworthiness limitations section unless the mandatory replacement times, inspection intervals, and related procedures specified in that section

notes.front: An engine reaches the removal time its manufacturer has set. Which reason for removal in the handbook applies?
notes.back: Engine or component lifespan exceeded.
notes.explanation: The handbook places manufacturer-set removal times and TBO under this reason.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine or Component Lifespan Exceeded”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: Thus, the manufacturer sets engine removal times.

notes.front: While a piston aeroplane taxis at low rpm, its propeller clips a toolbox; the engine keeps running. Which of the handbook’s reasons for removal governs the follow-up inspection?
notes.back: C: Sudden reduction in speed
notes.explanation: A blade striking an object at low rpm, with the engine recovering and running on, is the handbook’s sudden reduction in speed.
notes.choices:
A) Engine sudden stoppage
B) Engine or component lifespan exceeded
C) Sudden reduction in speed
D) Spectrometric oil analysis results
notes.choicesExplained: A requires rpm to reach zero in under one revolution. B concerns removal times. D concerns oil sample results, not a strike.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Sudden Reduction in Speed”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: While taxiing an aircraft, sudden reduction in speed can occur when the propeller strikes a foreign object, such as a raised section in the runway, a tool box, or a portion of another airplane.

notes.front: After a propeller strike, the strained oil shows only particles like fine filings. What does the handbook say to do?
notes.back: Continue the inspection of the engine to determine its serviceability.
notes.explanation: Fine filings do not by themselves mean removal, unlike heavy particles.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Sudden Reduction in Speed”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: However, if the metal particles present are similar to fine filings, continue the inspection of the engine to determine its serviceability.

notes.front: Successive oil samples show a wear metal rising beyond its normal rate. What can then follow?
notes.back: The operator can be notified quickly so that repair, a recommended specific maintenance procedure, or inspection can be ordered.
notes.explanation: Recording the wear metals at each sample is what reveals the abnormal rate.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spectrometric Oil Analysis Engine Inspection Program”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: The amount of wear metals is recorded and noted each time a sample is taken. If the amount of wear metals increases beyond a normal rate, then the operator can be notified quickly so repair, a recommended specific maintenance procedure, or inspection can be ordered.

notes.front: While torquing the engine mount nuts, a mechanic lets the hoist go slack so the engine bears on the bolts. What is the risk the handbook describes?
notes.back: The nuts pull the engine into alignment and reach torque without actually holding the engine securely.
notes.explanation: Letting the engine bear on the bolts is what produces torque without a secure hold.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Hoisting & Mounting the Engine for Installation”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: If the engine is permitted to exert upward or downward pressure on the bolts, it is necessary for the nuts to pull the engine into proper alignment. This results in nuts being tightened to the proper torque value without actually holding the engine securely to the aircraft.

notes.front: After the ground run-up and test flight of a newly installed engine, what should a mechanic especially check the oil system hose clamps for?
notes.back: Security, as shown by oil leakage at the hose connections.
notes.explanation: The handbook asks for all lines to be checked for leakage and security, and the oil hose clamps especially.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Checks & Adjustments After Engine Runup & Operation”, p. 8-13
notes.evidence: Check all lines for leakage and security of attachment. Especially, check the oil system hose clamps for security as evidenced by oil leakage at the hose connections.

notes.front: On a twin, one throttle has noticeably more cushion than the other. What does the handbook require, and why?
notes.back: Equal cushion on all engine controls on each quadrant, so all are aligned at any chosen setting.
notes.explanation: Equal cushion removes the need to set each control individually to synchronise the engines.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Connections & Adjustments”, p. 8-12
notes.evidence: On multiengine aircraft, the amount of cushion of all engine controls on each quadrant must be equal so that all are aligned at any specific setting chosen. This eliminates the necessity of setting each control individually to synchronize engine operations.

notes.front: During rigging, safety wire passes through the test hole in a control rod end. What does that show?
notes.back: The rod end terminal is not being held by the required number of threads.
notes.explanation: The test hole is provided in the shank for exactly this inspection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Disconnection of Engine Controls”, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: Most control rod ends are provided with a test hole in the shank for inspection. If safety wire can be inserted through the test hole, the terminal is not being held by the required number of threads.

notes.front: A mechanic proposes ordinary bolts in place of the special heat-treated steel bolts that secure an engine mount. Why does the handbook rule this out?
notes.back: Those special bolts alone support the entire weight of, and withstand all stresses from, the engine and propeller in flight.
notes.explanation: Only the specified bolts are meant to carry the full load of engine and propeller.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Mounts for Turbofan Engines”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: The engine mounts are usually secured to the aircraft by special heat-treated steel bolts. The importance of using only these special bolts can be readily appreciated, since they alone support the entire weight of, and withstand all, the stresses imposed by the engine and propeller in flight.

notes.front: An engine is attached by mount units whose pads are all angled to point at the centre of gravity of the engine’s mass. What type of mount are they?
notes.back: Dynafocal mounts.
notes.explanation: Pads angled at the engine’s centre of gravity are the defining feature of the dynafocal mount.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Mounts for Reciprocating Engines”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: Dynafocal engine mounts have the mounting pad angled to point to the CG of the engines mass.

notes.front: On a sudden-stoppage inspection, what does AC 43.13-1B say to examine the engine flex mounts for?
notes.back: Looseness of engine to mount, distortion, or signs of wear.
notes.explanation: This is the first item of the AC’s engine-mount inspection.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-2f, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: (1) Examine the engine flex mounts, when applicable, for looseness of engine to mount, distortion, or signs of wear.

notes.front: A mechanic plans to do a compression test the morning after a flight rather than straight after shutdown. What does the handbook advise?
notes.back: Test as soon as possible after shutdown, while the piston rings, cylinder walls and other parts are still freshly lubricated.
notes.explanation: Freshly lubricated parts are the condition the handbook wants for the test.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Compression Tests”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: Perform a compression test as soon as possible after the engine is shut down so that piston rings, cylinder walls, and other parts are still freshly lubricated.

notes.front: During a differential test, a mechanic turns the propeller past top dead centre. What does the handbook say to do?
notes.back: Back the propeller up at least one blade, then turn it again in the direction of rotation.
notes.explanation: Past top dead centre, the 15 to 20 psi in the cylinder tends to move the propeller in the direction of rotation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Differential Pressure Tester”, p. 10-40
notes.evidence: If the engine is rotated past top dead center, the 15 to 20 psi tends to move the propeller in the direction of rotation. If this occurs, back the propeller up at least one blade prior to turning the propeller again in the direction of rotation.

notes.front: With 80 psi regulated input, a hot cylinder’s gauge reads 56 psi. Applying AC 43.13-1B’s 25 percent guidance, what should the mechanic do first?
notes.back: A: Suspect the cylinder and recheck after running the engine for at least 3 minutes
notes.explanation: The loss is 24 psi, 30 percent of the input, which exceeds 25 percent and makes the cylinder suspect pending a recheck.
notes.choices:
A) Suspect the cylinder and recheck after running the engine for at least 3 minutes
B) Accept the cylinder: 56 psi is within limits
C) Remove the cylinder at once without a recheck
D) Raise the regulated pressure to 100 psi and retest
notes.choicesExplained: B: a 30 percent loss is over the 25 percent threshold. C: the AC calls for a recheck after running before removal. D: the test is made at 80 psi regulated pressure.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-14b(5)(i), p. 8-10
notes.evidence: A loss in excess of 25 percent of the input air pressure is cause to suspect the cylinder of being defective; however, recheck the readings after operating the engine for at least 3 minutes to allow for sealing of the rings with oil.

notes.front: With the propeller held at top dead centre and air applied, a mechanic hears air leaking from the air cleaner and carburettor heat box. What is leaking?
notes.back: B: The intake valve
notes.explanation: AC 43.13-1B ties leakage at the air cleaner or carburettor heat box to the intake valve.
notes.choices:
A) The exhaust valve
B) The intake valve
C) The piston rings
D) The spark plug adapter
notes.choicesExplained: A would vent through the exhaust pipe. C would show as air rushing from the dipstick opening. D is not a leak path the AC describes.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-14, p. 8-8
notes.evidence: If air is heard leaking out of the air cleaner/carburetor heat box, the intake valve is leaking.

notes.front: A mechanic opens the air valve to pressurise a cylinder to 80 psi, but the piston is short of top dead centre. What hazard does AC 43.13-1B warn of?
notes.back: B: The pressure can rapidly rotate the propeller
notes.explanation: The AC cautions that enough pressure builds in the cylinder to rotate the propeller rapidly when the piston is not at top dead centre.
notes.choices:
A) The regulator gauge will burst
B) The pressure can rapidly rotate the propeller
C) The cylinder will hydraulic lock
D) The spark plug adapter will blow out of the bushing
notes.choicesExplained: A, D and C are not the hazards the AC’s caution describes; the caution is about the propeller turning.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-14b(5)(f), p. 8-10
notes.evidence: CAUTION: Care must be exercised in opening the air valve since sufficient air pressure will have built up in the cylinder to cause it to rapidly rotate the propeller if the piston is not at TDC.

notes.front: A piston aeroplane noses over during taxi and its propeller stops within half a revolution. The engine manufacturer publishes sudden-stoppage instructions. What does AC 43.13-1B require before return to service?
notes.back: C: An inspection in accordance with the manufacturer’s maintenance instructions
notes.explanation: Stopping in under one revolution is sudden stoppage, and every such engine must be inspected per the manufacturer’s instructions.
notes.choices:
A) A new propeller and a ground run
B) An oil screen check only
C) An inspection in accordance with the manufacturer’s maintenance instructions
D) A 100-hour inspection
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are partial checks that the AC does not accept in place of the manufacturer’s inspection. D is a routine inspection, not the required sudden-stoppage inspection.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-2b, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: (1) Every engine that suffers a sudden stoppage must be inspected in accordance with the manufacturer’s maintenance instructions before being returned to service.

notes.front: How does AC 43.13-1B treat fine metal particles in the filter of a new or newly overhauled engine, compared with one that has run a while?
notes.back: New or newly overhauled: a small amount is not abnormal. After running and one or more oil changes: there should be no appreciable amount.
notes.explanation: The same finding means different things at different points in the engine’s life.

notes.front: How do the loads on the aft turbine vibration isolator mount differ from those on the forward mounts?
notes.back: The aft mount takes only vertical and side loads; the forward mounts also carry axial (thrust) loads.
notes.explanation: The aft mount still accommodates thermal expansion without putting axial loads on the engine flanges.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Turbine Vibration Isolation Engine Mounts”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: The aft mounts take only vertical and side loads; however, they will also accommodate thermal expansion of the engine without applying axial loads to the engine flanges.

notes.front: How do AC 43.13-1B’s 25 percent guidance and its 60/80 rule differ in what they require?
notes.back: A loss over 25 percent makes a cylinder suspect, pending recheck; under 60/80 hot, after corrective steps fail, it must be removed and inspected.
notes.explanation: The 60/80 rule applies only once the recheck and valve-seating steps have failed to raise the reading.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 8, para. 8-14, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: If a cylinder has less than a 60/80 reading on the differential test gauges on a hot engine and procedures in subparagraphs 8-14b(5)(i) and (j) fail to raise the compression reading, the cylinder must be removed and inspected.
